models.collectorNote: Split-window and oval-window early cars, and documented original convertibles, carry the original-Beetle market. The 1998-on cars are cheap used transport, not collectibles — yet.

generations.name: Original Beetle
generations.note: Production ran in Germany until 1978 and in Mexico until 2003. The engine grew from 1.1 to 1.6 litres; the idea never changed at all.

generations.name: New Beetle
generations.note: Golf mechanicals under a concept-car silhouette, flower vase on the dash included. Charm was the entire brief, and it landed.

generations.name: Beetle
generations.note: Flatter roof, turbo engines, a deliberate reach for male buyers the New Beetle never had. Better car, less magic, and the nameplate ended with it.

models.intro: The best-selling single design in car history — over 21 million originals. An air-cooled rear-engined economy car that outlived its century, then came back twice as nostalgia. The original is the one that matters.

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Giorgetto Giugiaro's folded-paper hatch replaced the Beetle. The GTI, launched 1976 with 110 hp in European trim, created a genre overnight.

generations.name: Seventh generation
generations.note: The MQB-platform Golf at its most complete: quiet, strong, and grown-up. The GTI and the all-wheel-drive Golf R split the enthusiast vote.

generations.name: Eighth generation
generations.note: Touch controls annoyed everyone; the cars underneath did not. The GTI makes 241 hp and the R is the all-weather answer.

models.intro: The Beetle's replacement and the car that defined the modern hatchback. The GTI variant invented the hot hatch in 1976 — a family car with a big engine and red trim that embarrassed sports cars — and every generation since has had to live up to it.
models.name: Golf

models.collectorNote: Samba prices detached years ago — six figures for the best. Honest Kombis and campers are the usable sweet spot; check the lower six inches for rust before anything else.

generations.name: Split Screen (Splitscreen)
generations.note: The split-windscreen original. The 21- and 23-window Samba, built to see the Alps through, is now the most valuable VW that isn't a one-off.

generations.name: Bay Window
generations.note: One-piece windscreen, sliding door, and the Westfalia camper conversions that defined road-trip freedom. Brazilian production of the type continued, in evolved form, to 2013.

models.intro: A delivery van that became a cultural era. The Bus carried hippies, surfboards, families, and half of Brazil — production there ran until 2013. Few vehicles have ever meant as much to as many different people.
models.name: Type 2 (Bus)

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: Audi-shared platform, Audi-grade cabin, and from 2001 the 4.0 W8 — two narrow-angle V4s on one crank, in a family sedan. Gloriously unnecessary.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Transverse engines again and a 3.6 VR6 option with real pace. The CC spin-off took the style brief seriously so this one didn't have to.

generations.name: Eighth generation
generations.note: MQB-based, wagon-led in Europe, and the last Passat generation sold broadly with a diesel heartland. Replaced by the wagon-only B9 in Europe.

models.intro: Volkswagen's sensible family car for fifty years — which produced some genuinely odd highlights, including a W8 engine nobody asked for. The US sedan ended in 2022, but the nameplate continues in Europe as a wagon and in China as a sedan.
models.name: Passat
